# allanninal.dev/build

> Diagram-first design walkthroughs of automations, DevOps, and cloud infrastructure by Allan Niñal. Each post is centered on a single architecture diagram with plain-language prose explaining how a small cloud system works end-to-end. Open to builds, collabs, and design reviews.

The site is a static blog hosted on GitHub Pages. Every post belongs to a 7-part series: 5 plain-language posts, 1 cost breakdown, and 1 dense engineering reference at the end. All systems described run on AWS for a few dollars a month at SMB volume.

## Work with me

- [Work with me](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/work-with-me/): How to engage Allan for a system design, a build, or a design review. Covers what gets designed, what an engagement looks like, who it's for, and how to start the conversation. LinkedIn is the only contact channel.

## Supplier bill matcher series

A serverless matcher that reads every supplier bill as it arrives, finds the matching purchase order and goods-received note, and checks them line by line for the right item, quantity, and price. Clean three-way matches clear for a manager's one-tap approval; anything off is flagged with the exact reason. It never pays a bill on its own.

- [A supplier bill matcher on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/bill-matcher-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a bill intake, a matcher, and an approval desk, plus the four outcomes every bill lands in: matched, price variance, quantity variance, or no PO.
- [How a supplier bill gets read](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-supplier-bill-gets-read/): Three lanes bring bills in — an emailed-PDF lane parsed by Textract, a supplier-portal poll, and a manual upload — and one Bedrock call per bill turns the raw read into clean lines.
- [How a bill gets matched three ways](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-bill-gets-matched-three-ways/): A plain-Python matcher lines the bill up against the purchase order and the goods-received note, checks item, quantity, and price against tolerances, and picks one of four outcomes. No model on the match.
- [How a mismatch reaches the right person](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-mismatch-reaches-the-right-person/): Routing per outcome, the right approver per supplier, a second sign-off for big spend, quiet hours, and an email carrying the exact failing line and the exact gap, with Approve, Query, and Reject.
- [How a bill gets approved for payment](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-bill-gets-approved-for-payment/): Three actions on every bill: approve (clear for the payment run, with a reason if it overrides a flag), query (send a templated question back to the supplier), and reject. Every action is logged; no bill pays itself.
- [What the bill matcher costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-bill-matcher-costs/): About $3.20/month at ~200 bills. The three-way match is essentially free; the cost is Textract reading each bill and one small Bedrock call per bill to clean the lines.
- [Engineering reference: the bill matcher architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/bill-matcher-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Weekly report builder series

A serverless builder that gathers a small business's own numbers — sales, new customers, cash in and out, top items — from the sources you point it at, compares them to last week and last month, writes a short plain-English summary grounded in the real figures, and emails it every Monday. It only reports facts from your data, never invents a number, and flags anything that looks off.

- [A weekly report builder on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/weekly-report-builder-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a gather step, a writer step, and a sender step — plus the one rule they all share: every number in the report comes from your data.
- [How the numbers get gathered](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-numbers-get-gathered/): Each source you list — a sales sheet, a Stripe or bank CSV, a point-of-sale roll-up — is mirrored to S3 on a schedule, then read and turned into one clean set of weekly figures with comparisons attached.
- [How the weekly report gets written](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-weekly-report-gets-written/): Plain Python computes every figure and every comparison first. Only then does one Bedrock call turn those real numbers into a short paragraph, and every figure it mentions is checked back against the data before sending.
- [How the report reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-report-reaches-the-owner/): The Monday send: the right recipients, the owner's timezone, a hold if the week's data isn't complete, and a composed email with the summary, the numbers table, and any flags.
- [How a number that looks off gets flagged](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-number-that-looks-off-gets-flagged/): Plain-Python checks catch a stale source, a figure far outside its normal range, or a total that doesn't reconcile. Anything that trips goes in a Needs a look section — shown, but marked unverified, never reported as fact.
- [What the weekly report builder costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-weekly-report-builder-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The builder runs once a week, gathers and compares with plain Python, and only fires one Bedrock call to write the summary paragraph.
- [Engineering reference: the weekly report builder architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/weekly-report-builder-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers: region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, EventBridge Scheduler config, the DynamoDB schemas, and the grounding contract that keeps the model from ever sourcing a number.

## Content moderator series

A serverless moderator that keeps a community page or comment section clean without a full-time moderator. Every new comment, review, or post is checked against your house rules; obvious-safe ones pass, clear rule-breakers are held for review (never auto-deleted), and borderline ones go to a human with the reason and the rule. It explains its calls and learns from each correction.

- [A content moderator on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/content-moderator-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an intake, a checker, and a review piece, plus the three calls they share for every item: pass, hold, or send to a human.
- [How a comment gets checked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-comment-gets-checked/): Every comment, review, or post arrives through one webhook, gets cleaned and stored once, and a fast rule pass settles the easy cases before any model is asked to look.
- [How a comment gets a verdict](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-comment-gets-a-verdict/): Only the borderline middle goes to Bedrock Haiku 4.5, which returns one of a few calls — pass, hold, or send to a human — with a confidence score and the exact house rule cited.
- [How flagged content reaches a moderator](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-flagged-content-reaches-a-moderator/): The review queue, who owns each area, quiet hours and batching so nobody is pinged at 2am, and the four guardrails between a held verdict and the review card landing.
- [How the moderator makes the final call](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-moderator-makes-the-final-call/): Three actions on the review card: publish a held item, remove it with the reason logged, or edit-and-publish. Removal is always a human's call, and every overturn teaches the system.
- [What the content moderator costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-content-moderator-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The fast rule pass settles most items with no model; Bedrock fires only on the borderline middle and the weekly digest.
- [Engineering reference: the content moderator architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/content-moderator-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers — region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SQS review queue, EventBridge config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Shift scheduler series

A serverless scheduler that takes the headache out of staff rotas for a small team. The manager sets who's available and the shifts that need covering; it drafts a fair weekly schedule that respects availability and hours, publishes it to staff once approved, and handles swap and time-off requests by finding a qualified replacement and routing the swap to the manager. It only proposes; the manager approves every schedule and every swap.

- [A shift scheduler on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/shift-scheduler-on-aws/): The whole system on one page: a week intake, a drafter, and a publish piece, plus the rule that the manager approves every schedule and every swap before anything reaches staff.
- [How a shift week gets set up](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-shift-week-gets-set-up/): Three lanes feed the week: the Drive sheet itself, a time-off note lane that reads plain-English requests into dates for one-tap approval, and a recurring template lane that fills in the standing shifts.
- [How a fair rota gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-fair-rota-gets-drafted/): A weekly run reads availability, hours targets, and skills, then places people into shifts by rule, preferring whoever is furthest below their target. It picks one of four outcomes per shift: filled, fair-swap, short-staffed, or held. No model on the draft.
- [How a schedule reaches the team](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-schedule-reaches-the-team/): Manager approval first, then per-person delivery, quiet hours, calendar invites, Slack DMs with each person's own shifts, email fallback, and the four guardrails between the approved draft and the schedule landing.
- [How a shift swap gets approved](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-shift-swap-gets-approved/): Three actions on a swap request: cover (find a qualified replacement, route to the manager), drop (give the shift back to the open pool), and time-off (hold the day for the next draft). Every action is logged and needs a manager yes.
- [What the shift scheduler costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-shift-scheduler-costs/): Pennies a month at small-team volume. The drafter runs once a week, calls no models on the draft, and only fires Bedrock on the time-off note lane and the weekly fairness summary. About $2.20/month at 15 staff.
- [Engineering reference: the shift scheduler architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/shift-scheduler-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn purely for engineers. Region, service names, resource identifiers, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Menu sync series

Keeps a restaurant's menu and prices the same everywhere. The owner edits one master menu in a Drive sheet; every change — new item, price update, sold-out, seasonal special — flows out to the website, the online-order platforms, and the printable PDF. Big changes wait for a tap; routine price syncs flow automatically within rules the owner sets; any place that rejects an update gets flagged.

- [A menu sync on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/menu-sync-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a change intake, a planner, and a publisher, plus the four moves they share for every item and channel.
- [How a menu change gets made](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-menu-change-gets-made/): Three lanes feed the master menu: the Drive sheet itself, a phone quick-edit lane for sold-out and small tweaks mid-service, and a supplier-price lane that parses forwarded lists into proposed prices for one-tap approval.
- [How a change turns into updates](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-change-turns-into-updates/): The planner reads the menu, diffs each item against what each channel currently shows, checks the change against the auto-sync limits, and picks one of four moves: in sync, push, hold, or flag. No model on the planner.
- [How an update reaches each place](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-update-reaches-each-place/): Channel resolution per item, the approval gate for held changes, per-channel formatting, idempotent sends, and the four guardrails between the planner's chosen move and the change actually landing.
- [How a rejected update gets fixed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-rejected-update-gets-fixed/): Three actions on a flag: retry (resend after a fix), edit (correct the value and resend), and skip (accept the channel can't take it, but keep it on the out-of-step report). Every action is logged.
- [What the menu sync costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-menu-sync-costs/): A few dollars a month at single-restaurant volume. The sync only does work on a change, calls no models in the planner, and only fires Bedrock on the supplier-price lane and the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the menu sync architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/menu-sync-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge config, the channel-adapter contract, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Tax doc collector series

A serverless system that takes the pain out of tax season for an accountant or bookkeeper. For each client it knows the checklist of documents needed, sends a secure request, collects uploads, checks off what arrives, and chases what's missing. It reads each upload just enough to confirm the right document type; a human reviews before anything is marked final.

- [A tax doc collector on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/tax-doc-collector-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a document intake, a tracker, and a dispatch piece, plus the four moves they share for every client file.
- [How a client file gets set up](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-client-file-gets-set-up/): Three ways a file starts: the Drive checklist sheet itself, a one-tap copy from last year's file, and a short intake form that picks the right checklist for the client type.
- [How a document arrives and gets checked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-document-arrives-and-gets-checked/): A client uploads on a secure page; the file lands in private storage; the collector reads it just enough to confirm the document type, matches it to a checklist item, and checks it off pending a human review.
- [How a client gets chased for missing docs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-client-gets-chased-for-missing-docs/): A daily tick reads each file, sees what's still missing, compares against the chase cadence, and picks one of four moves: complete, first request, reminder, escalate. No model on the tick.
- [How a finished file reaches the preparer](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-finished-file-reaches-the-preparer/): Three actions on a complete file: accept (the file moves to done), reject one item (the client gets a fresh request for just that item), and reopen (add a forgotten item back). Every action is logged.
- [What the tax doc collector costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-tax-doc-collector-costs/): A few dollars a month at small-practice volume. The chase tick calls no models; Textract and Bedrock fire only when a document is uploaded, plus the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the tax doc collector architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/tax-doc-collector-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Quote follow-up series

Makes sure a sent quote never goes cold. After you send a quote, it follows up on a sensible cadence with a friendly nudge, watches for the customer's reply, and stops the moment they accept, decline, or ask a question, handing those straight to you. It flags quotes about to expire and tells you which deals are still open. Never pushy; a person handles every real reply.

- [A quote follow-up system on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/quote-followup-on-aws/): The whole system on one page: a quote intake, a timer, and a sender, plus the way a reply stops everything cleanly and hands the deal to a person.
- [How a sent quote gets tracked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-sent-quote-gets-tracked/): Three lanes feed the open-quote list: the Drive sheet itself, an inbox lane that reads a sent-quote email into a proposed row for one-tap approval, and a webhook from your quoting tool.
- [How a follow-up gets timed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-follow-up-gets-timed/): A daily check reads the list, computes days since sent and days to expiry, compares against the cadence in the rules doc, and picks one of four moves: resting, first nudge, follow-up, last call. No model on the check.
- [How a quote nudge reaches the buyer](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-quote-nudge-reaches-the-buyer/): Owner resolution per quote, a draft written in your voice for one-tap approval, quiet hours and weekends, email send, and the four guardrails between the chosen move and the message landing.
- [How a reply stops the follow-ups](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-reply-stops-the-follow-ups/): Three outcomes when the customer replies: stop-and-hand-off (accept, decline, or question go to the rep), defer (out-of-office pushes the next nudge), and the expiry close-out. Every step is logged.
- [What the quote follow-up costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-quote-followup-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The check runs once a day and calls no model; Bedrock only fires to read a reply and draft a nudge. About $2.40/month at ~200 open quotes.
- [Engineering reference: the quote follow-up architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/quote-followup-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Social inbox unifier series

A serverless system that pulls every Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp DM into one shared queue so nothing is missed. It labels each message by topic and urgency, removes duplicates, and routes each to the right teammate, so a small team answers from one place instead of five apps. A human writes every reply; the system only gathers, labels, and routes.

- [A social inbox unifier on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/social-inbox-unifier-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — platform connectors, a labeler, and a shared inbox, plus the rule that a human writes every reply.
- [How a DM reaches the unified inbox](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-dm-reaches-the-unified-inbox/): Each platform pushes new messages to a webhook; a small connector verifies the call, turns every format into one common shape, and drops it on a single work queue.
- [How a DM gets labeled and deduped](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-dm-gets-labeled-and-deduped/): A fingerprint check drops re-delivered and cross-channel duplicates; one Bedrock call returns topic, urgency, and language. No model ever writes a reply.
- [How a DM finds the right teammate](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-dm-finds-the-right-teammate/): Routing by topic, working hours, fair load-sharing, and a backup — the four guardrails between a labeled message and the right person's queue.
- [How a DM gets answered](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-dm-gets-answered/): Three actions in the shared inbox: send a human-written reply, reassign, or close. Every reply goes back out on the customer's own platform, and every action is logged.
- [What the social inbox unifier costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-social-inbox-unifier-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The hot path is plain code; the only model call is one cheap label per new message.
- [Engineering reference: the social inbox unifier architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/social-inbox-unifier-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the webhook setup, SQS config, and DynamoDB schemas.

## Renewal negotiator series

A serverless helper that keeps customers at renewal time. Ahead of each contract or subscription renewal it gathers the current terms, usage, and history, drafts a tailored renewal offer in your voice with any discount inside your rules, and hands it to you to approve, edit, or skip before it reaches the customer. It only prepares the offer; a human always sends and can always override.

- [A renewal negotiator on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/renewal-negotiator-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an account intake, a drafter, and an approval queue, plus the rule that the system only ever prepares an offer and never sends one itself.
- [How a renewal gets prepared](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-renewal-gets-prepared/): Three lanes feed the account registry — the Drive sheet itself, an inbox-forwarding lane that parses contracts and usage exports into proposed rows, and an hourly calendar import for renewal dates tagged #renews.
- [How a renewal offer gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-renewal-offer-gets-drafted/): Plain Python picks the plan and the discount band from your rules; Bedrock then writes the offer in your voice. The model never sets a price or a discount — it only phrases what the rules already decided.
- [How a renewal offer reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-renewal-offer-reaches-the-owner/): Owner resolution per account, a discount-cap check that nothing skips, quiet hours, and the four guardrails between a freshly drafted offer and the moment it lands in your approval queue.
- [How a renewal gets sent or skipped](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-renewal-gets-sent-or-skipped/): Three actions on every draft: approve & send (the offer goes to the customer), edit (change wording, plan, or discount within the cap, then send), and skip (no offer this cycle). Every action is logged.
- [What the renewal negotiator costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-renewal-negotiator-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The daily check reads accounts with no model; Bedrock fires only when a renewal comes due and a draft is needed, plus the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the renewal negotiator architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/renewal-negotiator-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn purely for engineers. Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Feedback collector series

A serverless system that asks every customer how it went, at the right moment after a visit or purchase, with one simple question. It collects the answer and routes by it: happy customers get a gentle nudge to leave a public review; unhappy ones go straight to the owner privately so the problem gets fixed before it becomes a bad review. Quiet hours respected; it asks once and never nags.

- [A feedback collector on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/feedback-collector-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a request builder, a router, and a dispatch piece, plus the simple happy-or-unhappy split that decides where every reply goes.
- [How a feedback request goes out](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-feedback-request-goes-out/): Three lanes feed the customer list — the Drive sheet, a point-of-sale webhook, and an hourly booking import — then a timing rule picks the right moment to send one simple ask.
- [How a feedback reply comes back](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-feedback-reply-comes-back/): A one-tap star link hits a Function URL, or a short written reply comes back by email. The reply is recorded exactly once, the customer is marked answered, and the same ask is never sent twice.
- [How feedback gets routed by mood](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-feedback-gets-routed-by-mood/): A star tap is read by plain Python; a few words of free text get a quick Bedrock mood read. Every reply lands as happy, unhappy, or unclear — and that decides the next move.
- [How a review ask or a private fix happens](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-review-ask-or-private-fix-happens/): Happy gets a gentle, one-tap nudge to a public review link. Unhappy goes straight to the owner privately with the customer's words and a way to reach back. Unclear waits for a human. Every move is logged.
- [What the feedback collector costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-feedback-collector-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The system sends a handful of asks, reads star taps with no model, and only fires Bedrock on free-text replies and the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the feedback collector architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/feedback-collector-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers — region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Form intake router series

A serverless router that catches every form your website posts — contact, quote, booking, signup. It checks the fields, filters obvious spam, files each submission safely, and routes it to the right team and tool. If a downstream tool is down it retries and never drops the lead, and the customer always gets a we-got-it reply.

- [A form intake router on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/form-intake-router-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an intake door that saves and acknowledges first, a checker, and a dispatch piece, plus the shared design rules that mean no lead is ever lost.
- [How a form submission gets captured](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-form-submission-gets-captured/): A tiny snippet posts each form to a Function URL; the door saves the raw payload and writes a record, then acknowledges the customer before any slow downstream work. A submission key keeps a double-click from becoming two leads.
- [How a form submission gets checked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-form-submission-gets-checked/): Required-field checks and a layered spam filter that holds flagged leads for review instead of deleting them. Plain Python on the hot path; one cheap Bedrock second-opinion only on borderline spam and unknown categories.
- [How a form submission finds the right tool](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-form-submission-finds-the-right-tool/): A routing table in a Drive sheet maps each form to a team email, a CRM list or sheet tab, and an auto-reply. Each delivery runs as its own job on an SQS queue with retries, so a busy tool never costs a lead or holds up the others.
- [How a form submission gets confirmed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-form-submission-gets-confirmed/): The customer we-got-it reply on its own queued job, the retry budget and dead-letter queue that hold and replay anything a tool refuses, and the de-duplicate guard that stops double sends. Every finish is logged and replayable.
- [What the form intake router costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-form-intake-router-costs/): About $2/month at SMB volume. The hot path is plain Python and a couple of emails; Bedrock fires only on the few submissions that need a category guess or a spam second-opinion. No API Gateway, no NAT Gateway, no always-on compute.
- [Engineering reference: the form intake router architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/form-intake-router-engineering-reference/): Same system for engineers — region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, the Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the Function URL and SES ingress, the SQS and dead-letter queue config, the idempotency design, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Backup sentinel series

A serverless watcher that makes sure your backups actually worked — because a backup you never checked isn't a backup. It watches each backup job you point it at (databases, file stores, cloud drives), confirms each one finished, is recent, and is the right size, and warns the right owner the moment one is missing, stale, or shrank suspiciously. It only watches and warns; it never deletes or restores anything.

- [A backup sentinel on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/backup-sentinel-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a job intake, a checker, and a dispatch piece, plus the four states they share for every backup job.
- [How a backup job gets registered](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-backup-job-gets-registered/): Three lanes feed the job list: the Drive sheet itself, an inbox-forwarding lane that reads backup reports into proposed rows for one-tap approval, and a heartbeat lane where a job pings a private URL when it finishes.
- [How a backup gets checked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-backup-gets-checked/): A scheduled check reads each job's latest evidence, runs three plain tests — did it finish, is it recent, is it the right size — and picks one of four states: all green, warn, alert, escalate. No model on the check.
- [How a backup alert reaches its owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-backup-alert-reaches-its-owner/): Owner resolution per job, quiet hours, holiday calendars, Slack DMs with full context, email fallback, and the four guardrails between the checker's chosen state and the actual ping landing.
- [How a backup status gets cleared](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-backup-status-gets-cleared/): Three actions on the alert: mark fixed (the job ran clean again, resume checks), snooze (quiet it while you work), and mute (this job is meant to be paused). Mark fixed only sticks once the next check confirms a real healthy run. Every action is logged.
- [What the backup sentinel costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-backup-sentinel-costs/): Pennies a month at SMB volume. The checker runs a few times a day, calls no model on the check, and only fires Bedrock for the plain-English daily summary. About $1.50/month at ~30 jobs.
- [Engineering reference: the backup sentinel architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/backup-sentinel-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Transcription archive series

A serverless archive that keeps every call and meeting recording your business makes, transcribes each one, and files it by date, people, and topic. Ask a plain-language question and it returns the exact moment with a quote and a link to play it. Access is controlled and every search is logged.

- [A transcription archive on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/transcription-archive-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an intake, a filing-and-indexing piece, and a search piece, plus the way every recording becomes a findable, quotable record.
- [How a recording gets filed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-recording-gets-filed/): Three lanes feed the archive — a watched Drive folder, a forward-to-an-address lane, and a scheduled pull from your meeting tool — then Transcribe turns speech to text and a plain-Python step files it by date, people, and topic.
- [How a transcript becomes searchable](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-transcript-becomes-searchable/): Each transcript is split into short timed chunks, every chunk is turned into a vector by Titan Text Embeddings V2, and the vectors land in S3 Vectors so search can match by meaning, not just exact words.
- [How a question finds the moment](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-question-finds-the-moment/): A plain-language question becomes a vector, matches the closest chunks, gets filtered by who's allowed to see them, and Haiku 4.5 writes a short answer with a direct quote linked to the exact second.
- [How the archive stays private](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-archive-stays-private/): Access tags per recording, search results filtered before the answer is written, sensitive recordings kept out of open search, and a full search log of who asked what and when.
- [What the transcription archive costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-transcription-archive-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. Transcription runs once per recording and dominates the bill; embeddings, the answer model, and the vector store are small slivers, and there's no always-on compute.
- [Engineering reference: the transcription archive architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/transcription-archive-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, the Transcribe job config, Bedrock model IDs, the S3 Vectors index, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Photo tagger series

A serverless tagger that saves an online shop hours of typing. When new product photos land, it looks at each one and drafts the boring-but-important details — a clear title, alt text for accessibility, suggested tags and category, and a short description — so listings stay consistent and searchable. The owner reviews and approves; it never publishes a listing on its own, and it flags low-quality or wrong-looking images for a human.

- [A product photo tagger on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/photo-tagger-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a photo intake, a reader that drafts details, and a review piece, plus the safety rails that keep a wrong photo from ever reaching your store.
- [How a product photo gets read](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-product-photo-gets-read/): Two ways a photo gets in — a Drive folder and a direct S3 drop — then a resize-and-check step that shrinks the image and runs plain quality checks before any model looks at it.
- [How photo details get drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-photo-details-get-drafted/): One Bedrock vision call reads the photo and drafts five fields — title, alt text, tags, category, description — each with a confidence score, against the rules and word list in your style doc. No invented details.
- [How a bad photo gets flagged](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-bad-photo-gets-flagged/): Two layers catch a wrong or low-quality image — a deterministic quality gate before any model, and a model self-check that spots screenshots, receipts, people, and empty boxes — so a human looks instead of a bad draft going out.
- [How a listing gets approved](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-listing-gets-approved/): Three actions on every draft card: approve (write the fields to your store or an export sheet), edit (fix a word, then approve), and reject (send to a flagged folder with a reason). Every action is logged.
- [What the photo tagger costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-photo-tagger-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The system runs only when a photo lands, and the only real cost is the one Bedrock vision call per photo that drafts the details.

## Waitlist manager series

A serverless waitlist manager that turns no-shows and cancellations into filled slots. For a business that books slots — a salon, a clinic, a restaurant — it keeps a waitlist; when a slot frees up it offers it to the next suitable person with a short claim window, rolls to the next if they don't take it, and confirms the booking. Fair order; no double-booking, guaranteed by one conditional write.

- [A waitlist manager on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/waitlist-manager-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a waitlist intake, an offer engine, and a sender, plus the four moves they share for every freed slot.
- [How a waitlist entry gets added](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-waitlist-entry-gets-added/): Three lanes feed the list: the Drive sheet itself, an inbox-forwarding lane that parses booking requests into proposed rows for approval, and a web form that drops new entries straight in.
- [How a freed slot gets noticed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-freed-slot-gets-noticed/): A cancellation, a no-show, or a new opening comes in; the engine finds who fits, sorts them in fair order, and picks one of four moves: nobody fits, make an offer, roll on, or hand back to staff. No model in the loop.
- [How an offer reaches the next person](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-offer-reaches-the-next-person/): Picking the next eligible entry, quiet hours, a text or email with a one-tap claim link and a countdown, and the four guardrails between the chosen move and the offer landing.
- [How a slot gets claimed or rolls on](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-slot-gets-claimed-or-rolls-on/): One conditional write decides it: the first valid claim books the slot, any later click is told it's taken. If the window ends unclaimed, the offer rolls to the next person. Claim, decline, and time-out are all logged.
- [What the waitlist manager costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-waitlist-manager-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The engine wakes only when a slot frees up, calls no models on the offer path, and only fires Bedrock on the inbound parsing lane and the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the waitlist manager architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/waitlist-manager-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, the conditional-write claim, and the DynamoDB schemas.

- [How a purchase earns points](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-purchase-earns-points/): A sale arrives, the earn function reads the rules doc, works out the points, and picks one of four moves: skip, add points, add points and announce a reward, or hold for review. No model on the earn path.
- [How a reward gets redeemed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-reward-gets-redeemed/): Look up the customer, show the reward and what it costs, and the four guardrails between a staff tap and the points coming off: balance check, confirm, one-at-a-time lock, and a logged, reversible ledger row.

Every action is logged.
- [What the loyalty tracker costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-loyalty-tracker-costs/): A few dollars a month at small-shop volume. The earn math and the redeem check call no models, and Bedrock only fires once a month for the owner summary.

## Event RSVP manager series

A serverless manager that runs the guest list for a small event. People register; it confirms each RSVP, sends timely reminders before the date, handles cancellations and a waitlist that auto-offers a freed spot to the next person, caps capacity so the event never oversells, and gives the host a live headcount. Guests can confirm, cancel, or claim an offered spot right from the email.

- [An event RSVP manager on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/event-rsvp-manager-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a register form, a guest-list keeper, and a messenger — plus the moves they share for every guest: confirm, remind, cancel, and offer.
- [How an RSVP gets confirmed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-rsvp-gets-confirmed/): Three lanes get a guest onto the list — the web form, an email reply, and a host import — and a single conditional write claims a seat only if the event isn't full, so two people can never win the same last seat.
- [How an RSVP reminder gets scheduled](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-rsvp-reminder-gets-scheduled/): When a guest confirms, the system books their reminders — a week out, a day out, the morning of — as one-off Scheduler alarms. Quiet hours defer any reminder that would land overnight.
- [How a cancellation frees a spot](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-cancellation-frees-a-spot/): One signed-link click cancels cleanly: the seat is released, the guest's pending reminders are deleted, and the freed seat kicks off the waitlist offer. Every step is logged so the headcount always adds up.
- [How a freed spot finds the next guest](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-freed-spot-finds-the-next-guest/): The freed seat is offered, not given, to the first person on the waitlist. A timed claim link holds it; if it lapses, the offer rolls to the next person automatically. Nobody is silently skipped.
- [What the event RSVP manager costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-event-rsvp-manager-costs/): A few dollars per event — about $2.40 at 200 guests. Most of the bill is the emails it sends; the rest is pennies. Bedrock fires only on the post-event thank-you note and a small host Q&A helper.
- [Engineering reference: the event RSVP manager architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/event-rsvp-manager-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the conditional-write capacity logic, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Sentiment monitor series

A serverless monitor that watches the mentions you point it at, reads the mood of each one, and tracks whether the overall tone is rising or falling. It sends a short weekly pulse plus an instant alert if something starts going badly, flags the angriest items for a human first, and only ever listens and reports.

- [How a mention gets collected](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-mention-gets-collected/): Three sources feed one queue: review-site feeds, a social-listening export, and your own comment webhooks. Each new mention is de-duplicated so the same review is never read twice.
- [How the mood of a mention gets read](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-mood-of-a-mention-gets-read/): One Bedrock Haiku 4.5 call per mention returns a mood score and a one-line reason. The score is stored; the rolling trend on top of it is plain Python.
- [How an angry mention reaches a human](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-angry-mention-reaches-a-human/): Two deterministic triggers, a single very angry mention or a sharp drop in the average, pass through four guardrails before an instant alert lands, worst item first.
- [How the weekly pulse gets sent](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-weekly-pulse-gets-sent/): A short Monday email built from three blocks: the mood trend, the standout mentions, and what changed since last week. One model call writes the summary line.
- [What the sentiment monitor costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-sentiment-monitor-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The cost is one cheap mood read per mention; the collector, the trend math, the alerts, and the weekly pulse are pennies.

A serverless relay that lets a small team serve customers in any language. - [How a message gets its language detected](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-message-gets-its-language-detected/): A message arrives by email or web widget, gets cleaned of signatures and quoted history, and the relay reads its language with a cheap first pass and a careful fallback for short or mixed notes.
- [How a message gets translated for staff](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-message-gets-translated-for-staff/): The relay masks protected terms, translates the message into the team's language with the cheap model, re-runs only the shaky passages on the stronger model, and shows staff the original and translation side by side.
- [How a reply gets translated back](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-reply-gets-translated-back/): The staff member writes the reply in their own language; the relay translates it back, shows a round-trip check of what it will send, and waits for a person to press send.
- [How names and prices stay exact](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-names-and-prices-stay-exact/): Brand names, product names, account IDs, numbers, and prices are locked behind placeholders before translation and restored after, so the machine can never quietly change a figure or rename your product.

## Ticket router series

A serverless router that reads each new support ticket, works out the topic and how urgent it is, tags it, and routes it to the right team or person — flagging anything angry or urgent to jump the queue. It only sorts and routes; it never answers the customer itself. A misroute is one click for a human to fix, and the router learns the correction.

- [A ticket router on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/ticket-router-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a ticket intake, a router, and a hand-off piece, plus the four moves they share for every new ticket.
- [How a ticket gets read](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-ticket-gets-read/): Three lanes feed one queue — an email inbox, a web form, and a chat lane — then one small Bedrock Haiku 4.5 call reads the topic, the urgency, and the tone.
- [How a ticket gets routed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-ticket-gets-routed/): The router takes the topic, urgency, and tone, checks the rules and the VIP list, and picks one of four moves: route, priority, escalate, or hold. Plain Python, no model on the decision.
- [How a ticket reaches the right team](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-ticket-reaches-the-right-team/): Team resolution per topic, a priority lane that jumps the queue, a duplicate check, a Slack ping with full context, an email fallback, and the four guardrails on every hand-off.
- [How a misroute gets corrected](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-misroute-gets-corrected/): Three actions on a routed ticket: reassign (move it and teach the router), bump priority (raise or drop the urgency), and split (one ticket, two topics). Every action is logged and feeds the examples.
- [What the ticket router costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-ticket-router-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The only real cost is one small model call per ticket to read it; everything else is pennies. No always-on compute, no API Gateway.

## Churn predictor series

Spots customers who are quietly drifting away before they leave. It watches simple signals you already have — last order, support mood, login gaps — scores who looks at-risk with plain, explainable rules, and gives the owner a short weekly "reach out to these five" list with the reason for each. It only flags and explains; it never messages customers on its own.

- [A churn predictor on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/churn-predictor-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a signals intake, a scorer, and a hand-off piece, plus the four outcomes they share for every customer.
- [How an at-risk customer gets watched](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-at-risk-customer-gets-watched/): Three lanes feed the customer list: the Drive sheet itself, a daily order-feed import that refreshes last order and pace, and a support-inbox lane that reads each ticket's mood.
- [How a churn score gets calculated](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-churn-score-gets-calculated/): A weekly run turns each signal into points using weights in the rules doc, adds them up, and picks one of four bands: steady, watch, at-risk, churning. Plain arithmetic, no black box.
- [How an at-risk list reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-at-risk-list-reaches-the-owner/): Owner lookup per customer, a cap of five names a week, a plain reason per name, Slack or email delivery, and the four guardrails between the score and the list landing.
- [How a win-back gets tracked](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-win-back-gets-tracked/): Three actions per name: reached out (log and pause re-flagging), won back (mark the save and reset to steady), and lost (record the churn with a reason). Every action is logged.
- [What the churn predictor costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-churn-predictor-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The scorer runs once a week, calls no model on the hot path, and only fires Bedrock on the support-mood lane and the weekly reason write-up.
- [Engineering reference: the churn predictor architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/churn-predictor-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers: service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Compliance tracker series

A serverless tracker that keeps a small business on top of its recurring compliance tasks — the checks that happen on a rhythm, like a monthly safety check or an annual policy sign-off. It reminds the right owner when each is due, collects a quick note or file as proof, and shows a simple done-and-overdue board. The owner can mark done, attach evidence, or snooze right from the reminder.

- [A compliance tracker on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/compliance-tracker-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a task intake, a scheduler, and a reminder piece, plus the four moves they share for every recurring task.
- [How a compliance task gets set up](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-compliance-task-gets-set-up/): Three lanes feed the task list: the Drive sheet itself, a starter-pack lane that loads common controls for your industry, and an inbox-forwarding lane that turns a forwarded policy into a proposed task for one-tap approval.
- [How a control comes due](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-control-comes-due/): A daily tick computes the next due date per task from its repeat rule, compares against per-task reminder chains in the rules doc, and picks one of four moves: on-track, due now, overdue, escalate. No model on the tick.
- [How a compliance reminder reaches its owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-compliance-reminder-reaches-its-owner/): Owner resolution per task, quiet hours, holiday calendars, Slack DMs with full context, email fallback, and the four guardrails between the chosen move and the reminder actually landing.
- [How evidence gets captured](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-evidence-gets-captured/): Three actions on the Done button: done (stamp the date, compute the next due date), attach evidence (a note or file kept as proof), and snooze (delay without dismissing, capped per cycle). Every action is logged.
- [What the compliance tracker costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-compliance-tracker-costs/): Pennies a month at SMB volume. The tracker runs once a day, calls no models on the tick, and only fires Bedrock on the evidence-reading lane and the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the compliance tracker architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/compliance-tracker-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers: service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Content repurposer series

A serverless system that turns one long piece — a blog post or a recording transcript — into a week's worth of short posts. It reads the source, pulls the strongest points, and drafts platform-sized versions in your voice, grounded in the original so it doesn't make things up. You approve, edit, or skip each draft; nothing posts on its own.

- [A content repurposer on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/content-repurposer-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a source intake, a drafter, and a review desk, plus the rule that keeps every short post traceable back to the original.
- [How a long post gets loaded](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-long-post-gets-loaded/): Three lanes feed the source store — a Drive folder you drop posts into, a forwarding lane for recording transcripts, and a paste-a-link lane that fetches a published post and cleans it to plain text.
- [How the strongest points get pulled](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-strongest-points-get-pulled/): The source is split into passages, each one indexed, and Bedrock picks the handful worth posting — every chosen point carries the exact passage it came from, so nothing is invented.
- [How a clip gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-clip-gets-drafted/): Each chosen point becomes platform-sized drafts in your voice — a thread, short posts, a quote-card caption — written from a voice doc and checked against the source before it reaches you.
- [How a repurposed draft gets approved](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-repurposed-draft-gets-approved/): Three buttons on every draft: approve (send it on or queue it), edit (tweak it in a pre-filled box), and skip (drop it). Nothing posts on its own, and every choice is logged.
- [What the content repurposer costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-content-repurposer-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The system only runs when you give it a piece, and the cost is dominated by the Bedrock calls that pull points and draft each clip.
- [Engineering reference: the content repurposer architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/content-repurposer-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn purely for engineers. Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, the S3 Vectors index, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Cart recovery series

A serverless system that wins back online shoppers who added items but didn't check out. When a cart is left behind, it waits a sensible amount of time, then sends a friendly, well-timed reminder (and maybe a second) with what they left, and stops the instant they buy or unsubscribe. Never pushy: it respects quiet hours and sends one gentle nudge, not a barrage.

- [A cart recovery system on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/cart-recovery-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a cart intake, a waiter, and a sending piece, plus the four moves they share for every abandoned cart.
- [How an abandoned cart gets spotted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-abandoned-cart-gets-spotted/): Three lanes feed one cart list — a storefront webhook that catches every add and checkout, a nightly Drive export a human can read, and a saved-link tag lane.
- [How a cart reminder gets timed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-cart-reminder-gets-timed/): A per-cart wake-up computes time-since-abandon, compares against per-size waits in the rules doc, and picks one of four moves: still shopping, first reminder, second reminder, give up. No model on the decision.
- [How a cart reminder reaches the shopper](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-cart-reminder-reaches-the-shopper/): Address resolution, quiet hours, a do-not-disturb check, a polished friendly reminder with the items and a return link, and the four guardrails between the chosen move and the actual email landing.
- [How a cart recovery stops on checkout](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-cart-recovery-stops-on-checkout/): The chase stops the moment they buy. Plus three owner actions: suppress (stop one cart), unsubscribe (stop an email), and write off (close it out). Every action is logged.
- [What the cart recovery costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-cart-recovery-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The system wakes once per cart, calls no model on the decision, and only fires Bedrock to polish a line and on the monthly summary.
- [Engineering reference: the cart recovery architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/cart-recovery-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SQS and DLQ wiring, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Price monitor series

A serverless monitor that keeps an eye on competitor prices so you don't have to. It checks a list of competitor product pages on a schedule, notices when a price moves meaningfully, and sends the right owner a short alert with the recent history. It only suggests; it never changes your prices, and it stays polite to every site it checks.

- [A competitor price monitor on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/price-monitor-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a page checker, a watcher, and a dispatch piece, plus the four moves they share for every watched page. Designed on AWS for about $2/month.
- [How a competitor page gets watched](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-competitor-page-gets-watched/): Three lanes feed the watch list — the Drive sheet itself, a paste-a-link lane that reads a page once and proposes a row, and an hourly catalog import — and each new page gets a saved price rule for one-tap approval.
- [How a price move gets noticed](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-price-move-gets-noticed/): A scheduled check fetches each page, reads the price with a saved rule, compares it to the last reading and the per-page threshold, and picks one of four moves: steady, first alert, repeat move, big swing. No model on the check.
- [How a price alert reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-price-alert-reaches-the-owner/): Owner resolution per page, quiet hours, a daily cap so a sale day doesn't bury you, Slack DMs with full context, email fallback, and the four guardrails between the watcher's chosen move and the alert landing.
- [How a price alert gets handled](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-price-alert-gets-handled/): Three actions on every alert: note (log a decision, keep watching), mute (silence this page for a while), and stop (drop the page). The monitor never touches your prices. Every action is logged.
- [What the price monitor costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-price-monitor-costs/): About $2.40/month at typical SMB volume (around 200 watched pages). The routine check calls no models; Bedrock fires only when a page layout changes and on the monthly summary. No API Gateway, no NAT Gateway, no browser farm.
- [Engineering reference: the price monitor architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/price-monitor-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Region, service names, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the polite-fetch policy, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Applicant screener series

A serverless screener that helps a small team handle a flood of job applications fairly. It reads each resume against the role's must-haves you write down, gives a clear yes/maybe/no with the reasons it found, and routes strong matches to the hiring manager. A human makes every decision; it never rejects anyone on its own and sticks to job-related criteria only.

- [An applicant screener on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/applicant-screener-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an intake, a reader, and a router — plus the rule that keeps it fair: it sorts and explains, but a human always decides.
- [How an application gets read](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-application-gets-read/): Three lanes feed one queue — an apply inbox, a careers-form upload, and a job-board export. Each resume becomes plain text, and the personal fields are stripped before scoring.
- [How an applicant gets scored](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-applicant-gets-scored/): The reader checks each must-have and quotes the line that meets it. Plain Python counts met must-haves against your pass marks and lands on yes, maybe, or no. The cut-off is yours.
- [How a strong match reaches the hiring manager](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-strong-match-reaches-the-hiring-manager/): Strong matches get a short summary and land in the manager's review queue. Four guardrails sit between a score and a routed candidate: dedupe, the fairness check, the summary, and human review.
- [How a hiring decision gets made](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-hiring-decision-gets-made/): Three buttons on every card: advance, hold, and pass with a reason. Every tap is the human's call and every tap is logged. Any screener label can be overturned; the screener never decides.
- [What the applicant screener costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-applicant-screener-costs/): A few dollars a month at small-business volume. One Bedrock read per application, Textract only on scanned PDFs, and no always-on parts. Where the dollars go and how the bill scales.
- [Engineering reference: the applicant screener architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/applicant-screener-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers — service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, the DynamoDB schemas, and the fairness controls as concrete design decisions.

## Meeting notetaker series

A serverless notetaker that turns a meeting recording into useful notes. Drop in an audio or video file; it transcribes the meeting, writes a short summary, and pulls out the decisions and action items (who owns what, by when), then emails everyone a clean recap. It only summarizes what was actually said, and flags unclear owners or dates for a human to confirm.

- [A meeting notetaker on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/meeting-notetaker-on-aws/): The whole system on one page: a recording intake, a notes engine, and a recap step, plus the rule that every line of notes traces back to something actually said.
- [How a meeting recording comes in](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-meeting-recording-comes-in/): Three ways a recording enters the pipeline: a Drive folder you drop files into, a direct upload link straight to S3, and an email-forwarding lane for the file your conferencing tool sends.
- [How the transcript becomes notes](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-transcript-becomes-notes/): Amazon Transcribe turns the audio into text with speaker labels; then two grounded Bedrock passes write a short summary and pull out the decisions and action items, each tied to a transcript line.
- [How the notes stay grounded](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-notes-stay-grounded/): Four plain-code checks keep the notes honest: cite-or-drop, owner resolution, date sanity, and a needs-confirm queue for anything uncertain. Nothing invented reaches the recap.
- [How the recap reaches everyone](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-recap-reaches-everyone/): The organizer gets a draft to approve, fix, or trim; only then does the clean recap go to the whole room. Three actions on the draft: approve, edit, discard, each one logged.
- [What the meeting notetaker costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-meeting-notetaker-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. Transcription is the dominant cost, billed per minute of audio; Bedrock fires just twice per meeting. No always-on compute.
- [Engineering reference: the meeting notetaker architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/meeting-notetaker-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers: service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the Amazon Transcribe job config, EventBridge wiring, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Deadline reminder series

A serverless reminder that keeps a simple calendar of every recurring obligation your business has to meet — payroll, tax filings, license and permit renewals, insurance and compliance dates. It reminds the right person early enough to act, with the right lead time per type, and escalates to the owner if one is about to be missed. The owner can mark it done, snooze, or ack-only right from the reminder.

- [A deadline reminder on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/deadline-reminder-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — a deadline intake, a checker, and a sender, plus the four moves they share for every recurring obligation.
- [How a deadline gets on the calendar](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-deadline-gets-on-the-calendar/): Three lanes feed the calendar — the Drive sheet itself, an inbox-forwarding lane that parses notices into proposed rows for one-tap approval, and an hourly calendar import for events tagged #deadline.
- [How a deadline comes due](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-deadline-comes-due/): A daily check reads the calendar, computes days-to-due per deadline, compares against per-type lead-time chains in the rules doc, and picks one of four moves: clear, first reminder, follow-up, escalate. No model on the check.
- [How a deadline reminder reaches its owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-deadline-reminder-reaches-its-owner/): Owner resolution per deadline, quiet hours, holiday calendars, Slack DMs with full context, email fallback, and the four guardrails between the checker's chosen move and the reminder landing.
- [How a deadline gets marked done](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-deadline-gets-marked-done/): Three actions on the Done button: done (roll the next due date forward, fresh chain), snooze (delay without dismissing, capped at three per cycle), and ack-only (silence this cycle without rolling the date). Every action is logged.
- [What the deadline reminder costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-deadline-reminder-costs/): Pennies a month at SMB volume. The checker runs once a day, calls no models on the check, and only fires Bedrock on the inbox parsing lane and the monthly summary.

Service names, resource identifiers, region, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Shipping notifier series

A serverless notifier that watches each order's shipping status — placed, shipped, out for delivery, delivered, delayed — and sends the right friendly update at every step, so the customer is always in the loop and nobody on your team has to lift a finger. When a delivery runs late, it warns the customer and the owner early. It cuts 'where is my order?' emails, respects quiet hours, and never double-sends.

- [A shipping notifier on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/shipping-notifier-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an order intake, a notifier, and a sender, plus the five moves they share for every order as it moves through each shipping step.
- [How an order gets watched](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-order-gets-watched/): Three lanes feed the order list — the Drive sheet itself, a carrier webhook that posts tracking updates in real time, and an inbox-forwarding lane that reads forwarded carrier emails into proposed status changes for one-tap approval.
- [How a shipping update gets sent](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-shipping-update-gets-sent/): A scheduled check reads the order list, compares each order's status to what was last sent, and picks one of five moves: nothing, shipped, out for delivery, delivered, or delayed. No model on the check.
- [How a message reaches the customer](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-message-reaches-the-customer/): Contact resolution per order, quiet hours, unsubscribe checks, a friendly email with tracking, and the four guardrails between the notifier's chosen move and the actual update landing.
- [How a late delivery gets caught](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-late-delivery-gets-caught/): Three things happen when an order passes its expected date: warn the customer, alert the owner, and log the delay. Each updates the order list and writes an audit row so nothing slips silently.
- [What the shipping notifier costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-shipping-notifier-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume — about $2.40 at ~300 orders. The check runs on a schedule, calls no models, and only fires Bedrock on forwarded carrier emails and the monthly summary.

## Refund handler series

A serverless handler that reads each refund request, checks it against your own written refund policy, drafts a clear and kind reply, and routes the easy ones for one-tap approval while sending anything out of policy or high-value straight to a human. It never issues money on its own; a person approves every refund.

- [A refund handler on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/refund-handler-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an intake, a checker, and a reply piece, plus the one rule they all share: a person approves every refund.
- [How a refund request arrives](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-refund-request-arrives/): Three lanes feed one queue — a help inbox that catches forwarded emails, a contact-form webhook, and a manual paste lane for requests that came in by phone or chat.
- [How a refund gets checked against policy](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-refund-gets-checked-against-policy/): The checker pulls the exact policy lines that apply, decides only from them, cites the line it used, and picks one of four outcomes: in policy, out of policy, high-value, or not covered.
- [How a refund reply gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-refund-reply-gets-drafted/): The drafter writes a kind, plain reply in your voice, quotes the policy line it used, and four guardrails sit between the draft and the person who approves it.
- [How a refund gets approved](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-refund-gets-approved/): Two actions on the approval card — approve and edit — plus a decline path with a reason. The money only moves after a human tap, and every action is logged.
- [What the refund handler costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-refund-handler-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The handler runs only when a request comes in, uses a cheap model for most cases, and reserves the heavier model for the few hard ones.
- [Engineering reference: the refund handler architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/refund-handler-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers — service names, the S3 Vectors policy index, Bedrock model IDs, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, the SES inbound rule set, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Onboarding guide series

A serverless guide that walks every new customer through the right first steps automatically. When someone signs up, it starts a friendly sequence of timed messages and tasks, watches whether each step gets done, nudges gently if someone stalls, and tells the owner who is stuck so a human can step in. It adapts the pace to each customer and never spams.

- [An onboarding guide on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/onboarding-guide-on-aws/): The whole system on one page: a signup intake, a guide, and a sender, plus the four moves they share for every customer.
- [How a new customer gets enrolled](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-new-customer-gets-enrolled/): Three lanes start a sequence: a signup webhook from your app, a Drive sheet you fill in by hand, and an inbox-forwarding lane that reads a welcome email into a proposed row for one-tap approval.
- [How an onboarding step comes due](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-onboarding-step-comes-due/): A daily tick computes days-since-signup, checks which steps are done, compares against the per-plan step plan, and picks one of four moves: on track, next step due, gentle nudge, or flag to owner. No model on the tick.
- [How a nudge reaches a customer](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-nudge-reaches-a-customer/): Channel resolution, quiet hours, weekends, an email with the next step and a one-click done link, and the four guardrails between the guide's chosen move and the message landing.
- [How an onboarding finishes](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-onboarding-finishes/): Three ways a sequence ends: finish (all steps done, send a wrap-up), pause (hold the sequence without dropping the customer), and hand off (a human takes over). Every action is logged.
- [What the onboarding guide costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-onboarding-guide-costs/): Pennies a month at SMB volume. The guide runs once a day, calls no models on the tick, and only fires Bedrock on the occasional rewrite and the monthly summary.

## Survey analyzer series

A serverless analyzer that makes sense of open-ended survey answers. It reads every free-text response, groups them into the handful of themes people actually raised, counts each theme, pulls a representative quote, and emails the owner a short summary. Anything urgent gets flagged for a human right away.

- [A survey analyzer on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/survey-analyzer-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an answer intake, a grouping piece, and a summary piece, plus the urgent lane that jumps the queue for anything that can't wait.
- [How a survey answer gets collected](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-survey-answer-gets-collected/): Three lanes feed the answer store — a form-submit lane that posts each response the moment it's sent, an inbox-forwarding lane for email replies and exports, and a Drive sheet you paste exports into.
- [How answers get grouped into themes](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-answers-get-grouped-into-themes/): A weekly pass turns each answer into a vector with Titan embeddings, clusters the vectors with plain code, then asks Haiku to name each cluster and pick one real quote. The math is deterministic; the model only labels.
- [How a summary reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-summary-reaches-the-owner/): Sonnet writes a short summary from the grouped themes — never from one cherry-picked answer — and four guardrails check every count and quote before the weekly email lands in the owner's inbox.
- [How an urgent answer gets flagged](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-an-urgent-answer-gets-flagged/): Every answer runs a quick urgent check the moment it lands. An angry customer, a threat to leave, or a safety or legal concern jumps the weekly queue and goes straight to a human via SNS. Each flag is logged.
- [What the survey analyzer costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-survey-analyzer-costs/): A few dollars a month at SMB volume. The grouping pass runs once a week, the urgent check uses the cheap model on each answer, and the summary is one larger call — so the bill stays small.
- [Engineering reference: the survey analyzer architecture](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/survey-analyzer-engineering-reference/): Same system, drawn for engineers. Service names, region, Bedrock model IDs, the S3 Vectors index, Lambda inventory, IAM scopes, EventBridge Scheduler config, and the DynamoDB schemas.

## Newsletter composer series

A serverless composer that gathers the week's new blog posts, product notes, and wins from the sources you point it at, drafts a clear, friendly email issue in your voice grounded in those items, and hands it to the owner to approve, edit, or skip before it sends. Never sends without sign-off.

- [A newsletter composer on AWS for a few dollars a month](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/newsletter-composer-on-aws/): The whole system on one page — an item intake, a composer, and a sending piece, plus the four moves they share for every weekly run.
- [How a newsletter gathers the week's updates](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-newsletter-gathers-the-weeks-updates/): Three lanes feed one item pool — the Drive sheet where anyone drops a win, a feed lane that watches your blog's RSS, and an inbox-forwarding lane that turns a forwarded update into a proposed item for one-tap approval.
- [How a newsletter issue gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-newsletter-issue-gets-drafted/): A weekly run counts the fresh items, decides whether there's enough to send, then drafts the issue grounded only in those items and your voice doc. Five steps pick one of four moves: skip, draft, redraft, ready.
- [How a newsletter draft reaches the owner](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-newsletter-draft-reaches-the-owner/): Reviewer resolution, quiet hours, the grounding check that flags anything unsourced, the full draft in context, and the four guardrails between the finished draft and the review message landing.
- [How a newsletter issue gets approved and sent](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-a-newsletter-issue-gets-approved-and-sent/): Three actions on the review message: approve (queue to send after a cooling-off window), edit (open the draft, change it, re-submit), and skip (don't send this week). Every action is logged.
- [What the newsletter composer costs](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/what-the-newsletter-composer-costs/): A couple of dollars a month at SMB volume. The composer runs once a week, drafts with one Bedrock call, and sends one email per subscriber through SES.

Clusters that cross a repeat threshold become candidates. Plain Python over the vectors.
- [How the FAQ answer gets drafted](https://www.allanninal.dev/build/how-the-faq-answer-gets-drafted/): The drafter pulls the matching passages from your help docs, asks the model for a short answer grounded in those passages, and makes it cite a source.
